lesson.opening: A premise and a conclusion are roles within an argument, not permanent kinds of sentence. A claim can be the conclusion of one inference and a premise in the next.

sections.heading: The architecture of support
sections.body:
Consider: Every item in this box is catalogued. This coin is in the box. So this coin is catalogued. The first two sentences are premises; the third is the conclusion. They work together. Knowing only that the coin is in a box tells us nothing about whether it has been catalogued.

A longer argument can contain an intermediate conclusion. If catalogued items can be located in a database, the conclusion that the coin is catalogued can become a premise for the further conclusion that it can be located there. Argument maps make these dependencies explicit. An arrow means “is offered as support for,” not “occurred before.”

An unstated assumption is a claim the inference needs but the text does not explicitly provide. Recovering it can make an argument intelligible, but adding a premise changes what must be defended. Do not smuggle in whichever claim would make your preferred conclusion follow. Explain why the assumption fits the passage and identify it as your reconstruction.

Distinguish a challenge to a premise from a challenge to the inference. “Not every item in the box is catalogued” targets a premise. “Even if your premises were true, your conclusion would not follow” targets the support relation. Both may be serious, but they require different answers.

sections.heading: Reconstructing the argument
sections.body: The coin’s catalogued status is an intermediate conclusion. It depends on the first two claims and, with the database rule, supports the final conclusion. No claim about the coin’s age is needed.

sections.heading: A serious objection
sections.body: A critic might question whether every catalogued item has actually been entered into the database. That is a direct premise objection, even if the mapping is structurally impeccable.

choices: Every catalogued item has a database entry.

activities.prompt: Build the chain from policy to recommendation.
items: Items that are irreplaceable should receive protective storage.
Therefore this manuscript should receive protective storage.

activities.prompt: “This is a loaned object, so we must return it.” Which assumption completes the argument?
choices: Loaned objects must be returned under the relevant agreement.

activities.prompt: Which targets the database premise rather than the argument’s structure?
choices: Some catalogued objects have not yet received database entries.

activities.prompt: Can one statement be both a premise and a conclusion?
What does an arrow in a support map mean?
choices: The claim is offered as a reason for the target claim.
The target claim is certainly true.

activities.prompt: Reconstruct a short argument you encountered today. Identify an explicit premise, the conclusion, and one assumption you had to add.
activities.context: Every item in the blue box has been catalogued. The coin is an item in the blue box. So the coin has been catalogued. Every catalogued item has a database entry. Consequently the coin has a database entry.
rubric: I distinguish the speaker’s words from my reconstruction.
I show how the premise supports the conclusion.
I name an added assumption and explain why it is needed.
